commence operations in early 2027, the group’s Johor Bay project remains at the planning 
stage. Long-standing shareholders may recall that the original acquisition was announced in 
December 2012 and completed in September 2013, approximately 13 years ago.  
 
The 9.23-hectare site, originally known as Vantage Bay and subsequently repositioned as 
Vantage Bay Healthcare City, is located approximately one kilometre from the Johor 
Causeway. In the FY2026 Annual Report, management describes Johor Bay as a 26-acre 
masterplan anchored by a healthcare nucleus comprising a multi-disciplinary hospital, 
specialist suites, aged care living and healthcare-related facilities, alongside luxury 
residences, hospitality and commercial lifestyle components. 
 
The chairman also stated that a project of this scale must be carefully phased and optimised 
through appropriate partnerships and structures, with the objective of unlocking the 
potential of an asset held for many years. 
 
(i) 
Can the chairman clarify what substantive work has been completed on the 
Johor Bay project over the past 13 years, including planning, feasibility 
studies, design, regulatory approvals and engagement with potential 
partners or operators? To what extent does the current masterplan build on 
that work, and is the group effectively starting again from a new planning 
baseline? What has actually prevented the project from progressing over 13 
years, which constraints remain, and what specific conditions will finally 
trigger execution?  
 
(ii) 
Given the scale and complexity of the Johor Bay masterplan, is the group 
currently constrained by capital availability, development capability, 
management bandwidth or other resources?
qa.answer:
With the Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System (RTS) Link scheduled to commence 
operations in early 2027, the group’s Johor Bay project remains at the planning stage. Long-standing 
shareholders may recall that the original acquisition was announced in December 2012 and completed 
in September 2013, approximately 13 years ago. 
 
The 9.23-hectare site, originally known as Vantage Bay and subsequently repositioned as Vantage Bay 
Healthcare City, is located approximately one kilometre from the Johor Causeway. In the FY2026 
Annual Report, management describes Johor Bay as a 26-acre masterplan anchored by a healthcare 
nucleus comprising a multi-disciplinary hospital, specialist suites, aged care living and healthcare-
related facilities, alongside luxury residences, hospitality and commercial lifestyle components. 
 
The chairman also stated that a project of this scale must be carefully phased and optimised through 
appropriate partnerships and structures, with the objective of unlocking the potential of an asset held 
for many years. 
 
(i) 
Can the chairman clarify what substantive work has been completed on the Johor 
Bay project over the past 13 years, including planning, feasibility studies, design, 
regulatory approvals and engagement with potential partners or operators? To what 
extent does the current masterplan build on that work, and is the group effectively 
starting again from a new planning baseline? What has actually prevented the 
project from progressing over 13 years, which constraints remain, and what specific 
conditions will finally trigger execution?  
 
 
 
 

 
 
Response from Company 
 
The Group recognises that shareholders have waited a considerable time for the Johor 
Bay site to be developed. Over the years, considerable planning and development work 
has been undertaken, with the masterplan evolving to reflect changing market 
conditions, healthcare needs and the Group’s regional growth strategy. Development 
was paused during the COVID-19 pandemic. When the project was restarted in 2026, 
the Group reviewed its plans, as the hospital design prepared some years earlier was 
not optimally sized for today’s healthcare operating environment, which has shifted 
towards more outpatient care and fewer inpatient stays, with greater emphasis on 
preventive medicine, day surgery and enhanced recovery after surgery. In parallel, the 
Group has been actively working with a developer to activate the land, and further 
details will be announced in due course. The Johor–Singapore Special Economic Zone 
(“JS-SEZ”) and forthcoming RTS Link have further strengthened the site's strategic 
potential. 
 
The current masterplan builds on this earlier work, with substantial updates to the 
proposed Thomson Hospital Iskandariah to reflect the evolving healthcare landscape 
and care delivery models. In parallel, the Group has been engaging potential 
development partners for the wider mixed-use development, with a view to optimising 
the site's potential through appropriate phasing and partnerships. 
 
The Group remains committed to unlocking the long-term value of Johor Bay, while 
ensuring that development proceeds on a commercially sustainable basis. The focus 
is on finalising the appropriate development, funding and partnership structures before 
moving into execution, with due consideration for investment returns and the Group's 
broader capital commitments. 
 
(ii) 
Given the scale and complexity of the Johor Bay masterplan, is the group currently 
constrained by capital availability, development capability, management bandwidth 
or other resources?  
 
Response from Company 
 
The Group has the healthcare expertise to anchor Johor Bay, while recognising that a 
development of this scale requires additional capabilities in property development, 
project execution and financing. 
 
The pace of development has been shaped primarily by market timing, including the 
evolving specialist healthcare market in Johor, and the time required to identify and 
structure the right partnerships, rather than a lack of capital or management capability. 
 
Our strategy is to develop Johor Bay in phases, working with suitable co-investors and 
specialist development partners across the residential, lifestyle and aged living 
components. This will allow the Group to leverage external expertise and share the 
capital commitments and execution risks associated with the wider development. 
 
Importantly, we intend to maintain financial discipline throughout the project. Each 
phase will be assessed against its expected returns, funding requirements and impact 
on the Group’s balance sheet. Our priority is to unlock the long-term value of Johor Bay 
while preserving the resources and management focus needed to grow our core 
healthcare businesses

qa.answer:
Would the board and management provide shareholders with greater clarity on the following 
operational and financial matters? 
 
(i) 
Singapore: Can management help shareholders understand how the new Thomson 
Fertility Singapore (Novena) at United Square will fit into the group’s existing medical 
clinic and hospital network in Singapore? How does the facility compare in terms of 
capacity and scale with the group’s existing fertility operations? 
 
Response from Company 
 
Thomson Fertility Singapore (Novena) at United Square is the Group’s second fertility 
centre in Singapore, complementing our existing centre at Paragon Medical Centre. 
The expansion strengthens our presence in the Novena medical precinct and increases 
access to fertility assessment and treatment, while reinforcing our longstanding position 
in Singapore’s private fertility sector which spans close to four decades. 
 
While the new centre occupies a slightly smaller footprint than the Paragon facility, we 
have optimised the space to ensure we offer comparable treatment capacity and 
capabilities, allowing the Group to serve more patients across both locations. 
 
Both centres are supported by the Group’s wider network of obstetrics and gynaecology 
specialists, diagnostic services and Thomson Medical Centre, enabling continuity of 
care from fertility assessment and treatment through to pregnancy and delivery. 
 
The expansion reflects the Group’s continued investment in fertility as a core area of 
expertise, alongside the broader development of its multidisciplinary healthcare 
services in Singapore. 
 
(ii) 
Vietnam: Since 1 July 2025, certain consultations and treatments at FV Hospital have been 
eligible for 100% coverage under Vietnam’s Social Health Insurance scheme. Can 
management provide greater clarity on the scope of services covered and the 
proportion of FV Hospital’s patient base that could potentially benefit from the 
scheme? What increase in patient volumes, utilisation or revenue does management 
currently expect from the broader coverage, and over what timeframe? 
 
Response from Company 
 
FV Hospital has extended Social Health Insurance (“SHI”) coverage to all outpatient 
services since 1 July 2025 and inpatient services since 1 January 2026, subject to the 
applicable scheme eligibility and reimbursement terms. As Vietnamese patients make 
up the majority of FV Hospital's patient base, a significant proportion of patients can 
potentially benefit from this coverage. 
 
The extension of SHI is an important step in making FV Hospital's services more 
accessible and affordable by reducing patients' out-of-pocket costs. It also strengthens 
FV Hospital's competitiveness within Vietnam's healthcare market, where SHI is widely 
accepted across public and private hospitals. 
 

 
 
As this has been recently implemented, it is too early to take a view on the potential 
impact. We are closely monitoring this development and will adjust our approach along 
with the rest of our wider strategy for FV Hospital as things move forward.  
 
(iii) 
Leverage: According to the consolidated statement of cash flows, the group paid interest 
costs of $48.8 million in FY2026 and $61.0 million in FY2025. Debt and borrowings have 
also remained above $1.1 billion since FY2024.  
 
 
(Source: company annual report) 
 
Given the existing leverage, how much financial headroom does the group 
currently have to fund the Johor Bay project? In particular, what level of 
additional debt, if any, could the group take on while remaining within its target 
gearing and liquidity parameters, and as management considers potential 
strategic or joint venture partners, what proportion of the project’s capital 
requirements would it ideally seek to have funded by such partners? 
 
Response from Company 
 
The Group recognises that leverage and financing costs are central considerations in 
assessing a project of Johor Bay’s scale. As highlighted in the question, borrowings 
remained above S$1.1 billion at FY2026 year-end, while cash interest paid was S$48.8 
million, compared with S$61.0 million in FY2025. 
 
The Board’s approach is to evaluate Johor Bay’s funding separately by development 
phase, taking into account existing debt obligations, operating cash flows, committed 
capital expenditure and liquidity needs across the healthcare businesses. A structure 
involving development or financial partners could reduce the Group’s upfront equity 
contribution and distribute project risk. 
 
The Group will determine the appropriate mix of debt and partner funding for each 
phase once financing and transaction terms are finalised, within its prudent gearing and 
liquidity parameters

(i) 
Can the board disclose the formal search and nomination process undertaken 
before the nominating and remuneration committee recommended Mr Tong Kooi 
Ong’s appointment as chairman, as required by the SGX announcement 
template? In particular, what criteria and capabilities did the board identify as 
priorities for the role? 
 
Response from Company 
 
Mr Tong Kooi Ong was appointed Independent Non-Executive Chairman with effect 
from 1 February 2026, succeeding Mr Ng Ser Miang, who had chaired the Board since 
2015. 
 
In considering several candidates for the role, the Nominating and Remuneration 
Committee (NRC) placed particular emphasis on the experience and capabilities 
needed to guide the Group through its next phase of growth. These included strong 
business leadership, experience in managing large-scale and capital-intensive 
investments, and a deep understanding of the markets in which the Group operates. 
 
Mr Tong stood out for his extensive business track record and strong standing in 
Malaysia, a key market for the Group given its hospital operations and significant long-
term investments, including the Johor Bay development within the Johor–Singapore 
Special Economic Zone. 
 
His experience spans banking, media, building products and property development, 
including founding PhileoAllied Bank and The Edge Media Group, and serving as 
Executive Chairman of SGX-listed Avarga Limited. In particular, his experience in 
property development, capital allocation and managing complex businesses is directly 
relevant to the Group's strategic priorities. His established relationships in Malaysia's 
business community and understanding of the regional landscape further strengthen 
the perspective he brings to the Board. 
 
The NRC considered these capabilities against the requirements of the role and 
recommended Mr Tong as the preferred candidate. 
 
Mr Tong voluntarily waived his director's fee upon assuming the Chairmanship, 
reflecting his commitment to helping the Group strengthen its fundamentals and deliver 
on its long-term growth plans. The waiver remains in place and will be reviewed by him 
from time to time. Any future changes to the Chairman's fees will follow the NRC's 
established process and be submitted for shareholders' approval at a general meeting. 
 
(ii) 
Generally speaking, can the board explain how it substantively assesses the 
independence of each independent director, beyond the director’s own 
declaration? In particular, does the assessment consider personal, professional, 
business or other relationships that a director may have, or may have had, with 
the company, its significant shareholders, management or other relevant parties, 
including the nature, duration and materiality of any such relationships? 
 
 
 
 

 
 
Response from Company 
 
The Board assesses independence through the substance of a director’s relationships 
and circumstances, alongside the applicable listing and governance requirements. A 
director’s declaration is an important starting point, but the NRC must also consider 
whether any relationship or interest could affect, or reasonably be perceived to affect, 
the director’s independent judgement. 
 
Relevant considerations include current and past business or professional dealings 
with the Group, its management and substantial shareholders, as well as the nature, 
duration and materiality of those dealings.  
 
For FY2026, the NRC reviewed the independence of the Independent Directors and 
was satisfied that there were no relationships that would deem them not to be 
independent. The Board accepted the NRC’s assessment, with the relevant Directors 
abstaining from deliberations on their own independence. 
 
Separately, it is noted that Mr Lim Wee Kiat is also seeking re-election at the AGM. The 
director’s profile is found on page 11 of the annual report.

performance assessed? 
 
Response from Company 
 
The Group has a clear division of responsibilities among the Chairman, Executive Vice-
Chairman and Group Chief Executive Officer. 
 
The Independent Non-Executive Chairman leads the Board and is responsible for 
governance, oversight and management accountability. 
 
The Executive Vice-Chairman, Mr Lim Wee Kiat, leads the Group’s long-term growth 
strategy and major strategic initiatives, including mergers and acquisitions and special 
projects such as Johor Bay. He has played an important role in the Group’s expansion 
across Southeast Asia and remains closely involved in strategic decisions through 
regular engagement with country management teams. 
 
The Group CEO, Dr Melvin Heng, is responsible for the Group’s day-to-day 
management, operational and financial performance, and execution of its strategy, 
including business growth, productivity, technology and talent development. 
 
Major strategic and investment decisions remain subject to the Group’s established 
Board approval processes. The Nominating and Remuneration Committee (“NRC”) 
assesses Mr Lim’s performance annually, taking into account his contributions to the 
Group’s strategic priorities and effectiveness in discharging his responsibilities. 
 
 

 
 
Mr Lim Wee Kiat is currently also the chairman of RSP Architects Planners & Engineers 
(Pte) Ltd, the President of Spanish football club (Valencia Club de Futbol, S.A.D.) and a 
board member of Singapore Olympic Foundation. His other directorships and principal 
commitments are set out below. 
 
 
 
(Adapted from company annual report; 26 directorships including group entities such as FVH Singapore Pte Ltd, Hatch Health Pte Ltd 
and Sasteria Pte Ltd)

Can the board confirm whether the executive vice chairman role is performed on 
a full-time or non-full-time basis? Given that his external commitments span 
different industries and geographies, could the director help shareholders 
understand how he allocates his working time across these responsibilities? 
Specifically, what proportion of his working capacity is devoted to the group?  
 
Response from Company 
 
Mr Lim serves as Executive Vice-Chairman, providing strategic leadership and direction 
for the Group. His primary executive responsibilities are with Thomson Medical, where 
he has played an instrumental role in the Group’s growth and expansion across 
Southeast Asia into a leading regional healthcare player, and continues to be closely 
involved in advancing the Group’s long-term strategic priorities. 
 
The majority of Mr Lim’s directorships are held within the Group’s subsidiaries, 
reflecting his responsibilities across its regional operations. The Board is also cognisant 
of his external commitments and, through the Nominating and Remuneration 
Committee (NRC), regularly assesses his ability to devote sufficient time and attention 
to the Group. 
 
For FY2026, the NRC was satisfied that Mr Lim had adequately discharged his

Company’s response to Q1 
(i) 
ESA’s revenue of S$23.6 million in FY2026 is reported in Note 4 to the financial statements as 
a single product line, “semi-conductor components”, because the design, manufacture and sale 
of burn-in boards is the activity from which substantially all of ESA’s revenue is derived. ESA’s 
other activities, namely the distribution of semiconductor back-end equipment such as vision 
inspection and test systems, and consultancy services to the semiconductor industry, do not 
individually meet the threshold for separate presentation. The Company does not disclose the 
split of ESA’s revenue by activity or by product type beyond what is presented in the financial 
statements, as this information is commercially sensitive and would be of use to ESA’s 
competitors.  However, ESA’s revenue for FY2026 was almost entirely derived from the design, 
manufacture, assembly and sale of burn-in boards.  
By geographical market, as set out in Note 4, S$15.4 million (65%) of ESA’s revenue came 
from customers in the PRC, S$3.8 million (16%) from Singapore, S$2.8 million (12%) from 
Taiwan, S$0.5 million (2%) from Europe and S$1.0 million (4%) from other countries. 
As stated in the Financial Review, the S$8.6 million (57%) increase in revenue was mainly due 
to increased demand for burn-in boards from semiconductor manufacturers, driven by strong 
demand for memory chips from the expansion of AI data centres in Asia. Revenue from 
customers in the PRC almost doubled, from S$8.0 million in FY2025 to S$15.4 million in 
FY2026. 
(ii)

28, the Group had one major customer in FY2026, Customer A, in the electronics and trading 
segment, whose purchases rose from S$2.3 million in FY2025 to S$9.4 million in FY2026. That

increase in revenue reflected higher volumes of burn-in boards rather than higher selling prices. 
The Company does not disclose the proportion of revenue from repeat customers, selling prices 
or product mix, as this information is commercially sensitive. 
On sustainability beyond the current up-cycle, the Board refers shareholders to Note 3.1(b) to 
the financial statements. ESA is a well-established operating subsidiary with about 30 years of 
history, through several semiconductor cycles. Burn-in testing solutions are increasingly critical 
because of the complexity of modern chip design and the growing role of artificial intelligence, 
automation and data centres, and ESA continues to collaborate with global customers to meet 
evolving technical demands. ESA has no borrowings other than bank overdrafts fully backed 
by cash collateral, maintains long-standing credit arrangements with suppliers and enforces 
stringent payment and receivables policies, and a significant portion of its trade receivables at 
year-end has been collected since the reporting date. ESA’s customer base spans the PRC, 
Singapore, Taiwan and Europe.  
The Board recognises the concentration risk represented by Customer A, which accounted for 
about 40% of ESA’s revenue and 11% of Group revenue in FY2026, and the AC monitors this 

3

customers on a consignment basis, and its customers are semiconductor companies which use 
the boards in their own burn-in testing. ESA’s customers are therefore the end-users of its 
products, and ESA’s visibility of demand comes directly from them, through the specifications, 
qualification and orders that precede each production run. The Company does not disclose 
details of ESA’s order book or customers’ forecasts.

and its distribution of back-end equipment on behalf of its principals, in compliance with the 
export control and sanctions laws applicable to it, and no breach has been identified by ESA’s 
management. 
(iv)

including ESA, as part of its ongoing responsibility to enhance shareholder value, and takes 
into account the Group’s financial position, the stage of development of each business and 
prevailing market conditions. The Board has no plans to announce in relation to ESA. Any

requirements of the Listing Manual, including shareholders’ approval under Chapter 10 where 
applicable, and to the admission criteria and chain listing considerations of the relevant 
exchange. Should the Board decide on any such proposal, the Company will make the

of the manager on 1 July 2026, succeeding the former CEO who had been in the

particular, how did the board assess the importance of retail industry experience, 
investment and asset-management track record, understanding of REITs, capital 
allocation capabilities and other skills that it considers critical to leading the 
manager and repositioning the REIT for its next phase of growth? 
 
The Board, through the Nominating and Remuneration Committee, conducted a 
structured search with the brief to find a leader who could manage and enhance a multi-
market, multi-asset portfolio; allocate and fund capital with discipline through the cycle; 
and work with the Sponsor and investors on the Trust's next phase of growth. Retail 
experience mattered but was weighed alongside asset and investment management 
track record, capital management experience and an understanding of REIT operations, 
including the alignment of the manager with unitholders. Ms Tan's over 30 years of real 
estate experience with major landlords and developers across various asset classes met 
these criteria. The Board also considered the transition following the former CEO's tenure 
of more than 16 years.

as the performance of the Trust Index was approximately 75% below the 
benchmark index as at 30 June 2026. As at 30 June 2015, the underperformance 
was approximately 1%. This represents a significant deterioration in relative 
performance over the past decade.

to the REIT’s strategy or operating model, based on her assessment of the factors 
behind the REIT’s past performance? 
 
The Board recognises that the Trust's relative performance has not been satisfactory, 
and Ms Tan's review starts from that. She took up her role on 1 July 2026 and the review 
is ongoing. We will update unitholders once the Board has considered it. Three priorities 
are already clear as follows:   
 
i. 
Portfolio performance: building on the successful repurposing of The Starhill in 
Kuala Lumpur, we will explore opportunities to upgrade our assets, particularly 
Myer Centre Adelaide and our Singapore properties, to drive rental income and 
occupancy; 
ii. 
Capital recycling: following the Wisma Atria office divestment above book value, 
we will assess non-core or mature assets and redeploy proceeds where the risk-
adjusted return exceeds our cost of capital and the alternative uses of that capital; 
iii. 
Working closely with the Sponsor: to evaluate pipeline access and create value 
in core markets. 
 

3 
 
 
(iii) Given the REIT’s current size, discount to NAV and acquisition capacity, what

We take a disciplined approach to growth and do not view acquisitions as the only avenue 
for creating value. While size matters, we have learnt to focus on the quality of the growth,

acquisition opportunities in our core markets which are strategically aligned and accretive,

On ROA and ROE, these are not the primary measures of a REIT’s performance. They

For individual transactions, the Board uses the actual funding cost and the impact on

Question: The reported average cost of debt excludes amortisation of debt-related transaction 
costs (and other fees). What is the all-in weighted average cost of debt? When evaluating 
refinancing, new debt or other funding options, does the manager assess funding costs on an 
all-in basis, including transaction costs, fees and other financing-related expenses? 
The weighted average cost of debt reported in Lendlease REIT's FY2026 financial statements at 
2.75% represents the average rate for the financial year FY2026.  It comprises the interest margins 
charged by the banks for the respective loan facilities on top of the base interest costs. Base interest 
costs are dependent on market interest rates, subject to locking in fixed rates via interest rate hedges.  
Lendlease REIT has hedged 68% of its interest exposure as at 30 June 2026. 
The weighted average cost of debt excludes the amortisation of debt-related transaction costs, which 
are the upfront fees charged by the lenders at the establishment of each facility. Such fees are 
capitalized and amortized over the tenure of the relevant facilities in accordance with applicable 
accounting standards. Due to confidentiality of the commercial arrangements with the banks, we are 
unable to disclose the level of these fees and therefore the all-in weighted average cost of debt (adding 
on these fees). We would like to highlight that the amortization of upfront fees does not impact the 
distributable income.      
When evaluating debt funding and refinancing opportunities, the Manager considers a range of 
factors, including the interest margin and the upfront fee charged by the banks (i.e. together the all-in 
rate), debt tenor, liquidity and lender diversification.

In FY2026, the group’s revenue increased by 36.9% year-on-year to approximately $38.4 
million, while gross profit more than doubled to approximately $7.6 million. Gross margin 
improved from approximately 13.0% to 19.7%, supported by higher-margin contracts, 
better asset utilisation and growing recurring income from investment properties. The 
group also returned to profitability, recording a net profit of approximately $2.4 million.

transport services, security and manpower services, and investment properties, 
contributing to revenue growth and margin expansion. 
 
(Source: company annual report)  
 
(i) 
Engineering services: Growth in engineering services was supported by a 
stronger order book and improved project selection, including offshore and 
marine grating contracts secured from an established client. What differentiates 
the group’s grating products and services from those of its competitors? To 
what extent did the wins reflect technical capabilities, product quality, 
pricing, delivery reliability or established customer relationships, and how 
defensible are these advantages? 
 
(ii) 
Transport services: Given the significant increase in diesel prices, how was 
the transport services segment able to improve its profitability in FY2026? 
Can management quantify the respective contributions from improved 
vehicle utilisation, pricing, changes in customer or service mix, and cost 
control?  
 
(iii) 
Investment properties: The group operates two dormitories with a combined 
capacity of 707 beds. What were the occupancy rates as at 30 June 2026 and 
the latest available date (such as 30 September 2026)? How did actual 
occupancy rates and average rates compare with management’s projections

qa.answer:
In FY2026, the group’s revenue increased by 36.9% year-on-year to approximately 
$38.4 million, while gross profit more than doubled to approximately $7.6 million. Gross 
margin improved from approximately 13.0% to 19.7%, supported by higher-margin 
contracts, better asset utilisation and growing recurring income from investment 
properties. The group also returned to profitability, recording a net profit of 
approximately $2.4 million. 
The improvement was broad-based, with all four business segments, engineering 
services, transport services, security and manpower services, and investment 
properties, contributing to revenue growth and margin expansion. 
(Source: company annual report) 
(i) 
Engineering services: Growth in engineering services was supported by a stronger 
order book and improved project selection, including offshore and marine grating 
contracts secured from an established client. What differentiates the group’s grating 
products and services from those of its competitors? To what extent did the wins 
reflect technical capabilities, product quality, pricing, delivery reliability or 
established customer relationships, and how defensible are these advantages? 
Company’s response to Q1(i) 
The Group does not manufacture grating. It is an authorised distributor for an 
established German grating manufacturer, and supplies its products according to client 

specifications for offshore and marine projects, where clients place emphasis on 
compliance with project standards, consistent quality and on-time delivery. The 
Group’s offering combines the manufacturer’s product quality and certifications with 
local project support, including advising clients on product selection, coordinating 
materials to meet project specifications, arranging cutting and fitting where required, 
and managing logistics and delivery schedules. The Group’s own storage yard and 
logistics capabilities allow it to coordinate the storage, handling and delivery of 
materials in line with clients’ project requirements, which is particularly relevant to 
offshore and marine projects with demanding specifications and delivery schedules. 
The offshore and marine grating contracts secured in FY2026 reflected a combination 
of product quality, competitive pricing, delivery reliability, logistics capabilities and 
established customer relationships, rather than price alone. Repeat orders from an 
established client show that our quality and delivery record has been accepted on prior 
projects. Pricing remains competitive, and the Group continues to tender selectively for 
contracts with better margins rather than competing on price. 
The Group has maintained established customer relationships in the oil and gas 
industry since 2015, spanning more than a decade, and has developed a strong 
understanding of clients’ technical requirements, operational expectations and project 
delivery schedules. We believe this industry experience, our operational infrastructure 
and our ability to consistently meet clients’ requirements are our competitive 
advantages, as offshore and marine clients generally prefer proven suppliers. In 
addition, as the Group also provides transport, security and manpower services, it often 
has existing relationships with clients across more than one business segment. These 
touch points give the Group a better understanding of clients’ wider operational needs 
and allow it to offer complementary services alongside grating supply. Having said that, 
the market is competitive, and these advantages must be sustained through continued 
operational performance, strong supplier relationships and competitive pricing. The 
Group will continue to focus on sustainable margins while strengthening existing client 
relationships and broadening its client base. 
(ii) 
Transport services: Given the significant increase in diesel prices, how was the 
transport services segment able to improve its profitability in FY2026? Can 
management quantify the respective contributions from improved vehicle 
utilisation, pricing, changes in customer or service mix, and cost control? 
Company’s response to Q1(ii) 
Transport services revenue grew 31.8% to $7.31 million and gross profit grew 58.4% 
to $1.48 million, with gross margin improving from about 16.9% to 20.3%. 
The improvement came mainly from higher vehicle utilisation, as additional contracts 
were served largely with the existing fleet, together with continued fleet optimisation, 
better route planning and stronger demand from commercial clients. As a result, 
revenue grew faster than the segment’s main operating costs. Driver salaries and 
related costs increased by about 12.4%, while repair and maintenance and insurance 
costs increased by about 2.4% and 2.6% respectively. Depreciation decreased by 
about $137,000, as more of the fleet became fully depreciated while remaining in 
service. 
To support new contracts, the Group also made greater use of subcontracted transport 
services, with subcontractor costs increasing from about $0.86 million to $1.79 million. 

Fuel expense increased from about $0.63 million to $0.85 million, reflecting higher 
diesel prices and the higher level of activity. Despite these increases, cost of sales 
grew by 26.4%, below revenue growth of 31.8%, resulting in the higher gross margin. 
These figures show the principal cost movements. However, the effects of vehicle 
utilisation, pricing and changes in customer or service mix operate together and are 
not tracked separately in a way that allows their respective contributions to be reliably 
quantified. Diesel cost remains a key sensitivity, and the Group takes fuel prices into 
account when pricing new and renewed contracts. The Group will continue to focus on 
securing contracts with healthy margins and managing operating costs prudently. 
(iii) 
Investment properties: The group operates two dormitories with a combined capacity 
of 707 beds. What were the occupancy rates as at 30 June 2026 and the latest 
available date (such as 30 September 2026)? How did actual occupancy rates 
and average rates compare with management’s projections when the 
investments were planned? 
Company’s response to Q1(iii) 
The Group’s two investment properties, Amethyst House and Beryl House, each 
comprise industrial space that is leased to tenants or used by the Group for its own 
operations, with about half of the space repositioned as a workers’ dormitory. The 
dormitories at Amethyst House and Beryl House have 299 beds and 408 beds 
respectively. As at 30 June 2026 and 30 September 2026, both dormitories were 
operating at close to full occupancy of above 95%, with vacant beds mainly arising 
from the turnover between tenant check-outs and check-ins. 
Amethyst House has operated at consistently high occupancy. Beryl House received 
its FEDA licence in mid-May 2026 and reached close to full occupancy faster than 
anticipated. 
When the investments were evaluated, the Board’s assessment allowed for a ramp-up 
period after licensing before occupancy stabilises. Actual occupancy and average bed 
rates have been ahead of those expectations. The investment properties segment 
turned from a gross loss of $0.50 million in FY2025 to a gross profit of $0.85 million in 
FY2026, driven by the Amethyst House dormitory and rental income from the industrial 
space at both properties. The industrial space at Beryl House has been leased to 
tenants since the Group took over the property in December 2024, but its dormitory 
began operations only after it received its FEDA licence in mid-May 2026. The Beryl 
House dormitory therefore contributed only about six weeks of operations in FY2026, 
and its full contribution is expected from FY2027

As at 30 June 2026, the group has $4.23 million in property, plant and equipment 
(PPE), $33.9 million in investment properties and no inventories. PPE comprises mainly 
$1.90 million in motor vehicles, and $1.93 million in scaffold equipment (Note 14 – 
Property, plant and equipment; page 74). 

(Source: company annual report; emphasis added) 
In FY2026, revenue increased from $28.0 million to $38.4 million. Over the same period, 
subcontractor costs rose from $902,000 to $2.43 million, while employee benefits expense 
increased by 8.8%, from $16.28 million to $17.72 million (Note 6 – Cost of sales; page 70). 
Excluding revenue from investment properties, revenue from the group’s other business 
activities increased by approximately $8.4 million. 
(i) 
Given the group’s relatively modest PPE base, how does it deliver its 
engineering, transport, security and manpower services at its current scale? 
What proportion of service delivery is undertaken using the group’s own assets 
and employees versus subcontractors or other third parties? How has this mix 
changed as revenue grew, and what controls does management have to ensure 
service quality, delivery reliability and margins are not compromised by greater 
reliance on external parties? 
Company’s response to Q2(i) 
The Group’s businesses are mainly manpower-driven, and its scale depends on its 
workforce rather than its PPE. The carrying amount of PPE also understates the assets 
in use, as a significant part of the Group’s bus fleet has been fully depreciated but 
remains in active service. As at 30 June 2026, motor vehicles in the transport business 
had an original cost of about $9.3 million but a carrying amount of about $1.2 million. 
Security services are delivered entirely by the Group’s own employees. Manpower 
services are also delivered mainly by the Group’s own employees, with subcontractors 
engaged to support peak-period deployment. Transport services use the Group’s own 
fleet and drivers, supplemented by subcontracted capacity to support new contracts. 
Engineering services use the Group’s own scaffold equipment and workers, with 
subcontractors engaged for specialised scopes and peak workloads. 
Our own employees remain the main delivery channel. In FY2026, employee benefits 
expense in cost of sales was $17.72 million, compared with subcontractor costs of 
$2.43 million. Subcontractors therefore accounted for about 12% of these combined 
costs, up from about 5% in FY2025. The increase was mainly in transport services, 
which accounted for about three-quarters of FY2026 subcontractor costs. 
Subcontracted capacity allowed the Group to mobilise new transport contracts 
promptly while it assesses whether their volume and duration justify further investment 
in its own fleet. The balance related mainly to engineering services, for specialised 
scopes and peak workloads, and to manpower services, for peak-period deployment. 
This approach allowed the Group to grow revenue without committing to additional 
fixed costs ahead of demand. 
To safeguard quality, reliability and margins, subcontractors are engaged from an 
approved list based on capability, safety record and past performance. Subcontracted 

costs are priced into each project and project margins are reviewed against budget. 
Subcontracted work is supervised by our own project and site personnel, who remain 
accountable to the client. 
As at 30 June 2026, the group does not carry inventory. 
(ii) 
Is this consistent with the group’s normal operating model, or does it reflect the 
timing of project procurement and delivery? For the offshore and marine grating 
contracts, who bears the cost and risk of procuring and holding materials, and 
what level of working capital is required to fulfil these contracts? 
Company’s response to Q2(ii) 
Yes, this is consistent with the Group’s normal project-based operating model. The 
Group does not generally hold stock for resale. Materials are procured against 
confirmed orders and allocated to specific projects based on their technical

2025 comprised materials which, following a review of its operating requirements in 
FY2026, the Group decided to retain for use in its own operations. These were 
therefore reclassified to property, plant and equipment. 
For the offshore and marine grating contracts, the Group procures materials from its 
German manufacturer against the client’s confirmed purchase orders and bears the 
procurement, holding and delivery risk until the materials are delivered to the client, 
subject to the agreed contract terms. This includes receiving the materials in bulk and 
breaking bulk at the Group’s own storage yard before delivery to the client’s site. This 
risk is mitigated by ordering only against confirmed orders from a reputable, long-
standing client, as described in our response to Q1(i), and by coordinating delivery 
schedules and closely monitoring project requirements. As the client pays upon 
delivery, working capital is required mainly for materials and labour between 
procurement and client payment. This is funded from internal resources, supported by

The internal audit plan is risk-based. Baker Tilly TFW LLP proposes the plan with

The plan covers the Group’s key business processes and entities over a three-year

Company’s response to Q3(ii) 
Yes. The ARC reviewed and updated the Group’s risk register during FY2026 to reflect 
the growth in investment properties and the dormitory business, and the internal audit 
plan was adjusted accordingly. 
The new or heightened risks identified include: a) financing and interest rate risk from 
higher property-related borrowings, addressed through Board oversight of gearing and 
monitoring of interest costs and loan maturities; b) property valuation risk, addressed 
through independent valuations and ARC review of valuation assumptions with the 
external auditors; c) regulatory and licensing risk for dormitories, addressed through 
compliance with MOM and FEDA licensing conditions and regular inspections; d) 
tenant credit and occupancy risk, addressed through tenant screening, security 
deposits and monthly monitoring of collections and occupancy; and e) governance of 
jointly-owned subsidiaries, addressed through shareholder agreements, board 
representation and the application of Group financial controls to these entities.

In FY2026, the internal audit covered IT general controls, human resources and 
payroll, and fixed assets management. No significant risk on the internal control system 
was brought to the attention of the ARC in FY2026. Recommendations for process 
improvements were made, and management has implemented or is implementing 
them, with progress monitored by the ARC.

the opinion that the Group’s internal controls and risk management systems were 
adequate and effective as at 30 June 2026.
